processing_steps.processing_steps_notes: Alloys processed by vacuum induction melting; as-cast terminal state (no further heat treatment reported).
Mould dimensions: 32 mm diameter × 186 mm length.
Mechanical test specimens cut from cast ingots by spark erosion, along the longitudinal axis (casting direction); specimen surfaces ground.

structures.overall_structure: Single-phase Fe3Al matrix with polygonal grains (700 μm); no dendrites and no precipitates reported for the binary Fe-26Al reference alloy.

interfaces.slip_behavior: Tension–compression asymmetry attributed to glide of screw dislocations with nonplanar (delocalised) core structure in bcc metals; Bauschinger effect from different elastic properties of matrix and secondary phases also mentioned as contributing factor.
interfaces.phase_evolution: Fe-26Al undergoes D0₃/B2 order–disorder transition at around 550 °C and B2/A2 at around 800 °C before melting.
interfaces.interface_notes: Binary single-phase Fe3Al matrix; no second-phase interfaces or precipitates reported for Fe-26Al.

measurement_conditions.specimen_geometry: compression: (6 × 6 × 10) mm^3; tension: flat (3.5 × 5) mm^2 cross-section, 15 mm gauge length
measurement_conditions.other_conditions: Specimens cut along longitudinal axis (casting direction); surfaces ground; ZWICK 1474 universal testing machine; Brinell hardness: load 62.5 g, indentation ball 2.5 mm diameter.

tensile_properties.stress_strain_curves: Compression: linear elastic part followed by parabolic hardening stage (Fig. 2b); tension: linear elastic loading followed by abrupt brittle fracture (Fig. 3b).

measurement_conditions.other_conditions: Samples held 30 min at testing temperature before loading; temperature checked by NiCr–Ni thermocouple on specimen surface; radiation furnace.

characterization_methods.instrument_or_setup: Brinell hardness tester (load 62.5 g, indentation ball 2.5 mm diameter)

characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: Room temperature and elevated temperatures up to 800 °C; deformation rate 10^-4 s^-1; specimens (6 × 6 × 10) mm^3; elevated-temperature tests in protective argon, 30 min hold, NiCr–Ni thermocouple.
characterization_methods.purpose: Determine yield stress in compression and its temperature dependence (yield stress anomaly).
characterization_methods.key_findings: Room-temperature yield stress 644 MPa; yield stress anomaly peak at ≈550 °C with ≈400 MPa; binary Fe-26Al weakest above ~600 °C.

characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: Room temperature and 650 °C / 800 °C; deformation rate 10^-4 s^-1; flat specimens (3.5 × 5) mm^2 cross-section, 15 mm gauge length.
characterization_methods.purpose: Determine room-temperature ductility and high-temperature tensile strength.
characterization_methods.key_findings: Room-temperature yield stress 475 MPa; total elongation 0.4%; very brittle behaviour.

characterization_methods.technique: Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) of fracture surfaces
characterization_methods.instrument_or_setup: SEM-Hitachi S-530, 20 kV, working distance 15 mm, secondary electrons (SE)
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: Fracture surfaces of tensile specimens after room-temperature testing.
characterization_methods.key_findings: Fe-26Al: very coarse transgranular fracture with a large smooth facet crossing the field (Fig. 4f); mode of fracture TGC.

unmapped_findings: Binary Fe-26Al is the reference alloy of the Fe-26Al-based series; Table 1 lists no precipitates for Fe-26Al (polygonal grains, 700 μm).

At room temperature in compression, the binary Fe-26Al stress–strain curve consists of a linear elastic part followed by a parabolic hardening stage (Fig. 2b); in tension it fails in a brittle manner (Fig. 3b).

Fe-26Al exhibits tension–compression asymmetry: yield stress in compression (644 MPa) is higher than in tension (475 MPa); the text states that the tension–compression asymmetry of Fe-26Al-based alloys is higher than that of Fe-15Al-based alloys.

At 650 °C the binary Fe-26Al yield-stress bars stay close to the 100 MPa tick and are the shortest among Fe-26Al-based alloys (Fig. 7); at 800 °C Fe-26Al shows the smallest yield stress (Fig. 8); no numeric value labels are printed on the bars.

In the elevated-temperature compression curves, binary Fe-26Al is strongest at room temperature (above the 600 MPa gridline) but weakest above ~600 °C, dropping to the 0–50 MPa range at 800 °C (Fig. 6).
Fracture surface of Fe-26Al after room-temperature tensile testing: very coarse transgranular fracture with a large smooth facet crossing the field (Fig. 4f); fracture mode TGC.
